why.say:
Okay, quick game: true or false, hands up for true. One, an adjuster's deadline can bend if you ask nicely. Two, a court's deadline can bend if you ask nicely.

{name}, I see you, your hand went up for number two. Bold. Honestly, I love the optimism, but no.

Here's where we are. Our 07/20/2026 Time-Limited Demand to Keystone lapsed unaccepted on 08/21/2026, and the 48-Hour Mandate got no answer. So Atty. Thorne made the call, and on 09/24/2026 John Doe's file became Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417.

From that day on, a judge sets the pace, not an adjuster.

So we keep two things. A Pleadings Log, which is just our running list of everything filed and served. And a Discovery Calendar, which is every date the other side owes us something, or we owe them.

Here's the one thing to carry out of this slide: once we file, the judge holds the stopwatch.

One warning before we go on. There's one kind of paper in this lesson that, if you ignore it, answers itself, and not in our favor. I'll show you which one.

The red flag on discovery is fifteen RFAs with no row of their own. An unanswered RFA may be deemed admitted. They get their own row, and Atty. Thorne hears within the hour.
why.ask: {name}, now that we're in suit, who decides the very next legal step, and who makes sure it actually happens on time?

theory.say:
Let me put it simply. A lawsuit is a strict, step-by-step process the court runs, and if we miss a deadline or misfile something, the court can throw the case out.

Your job shifts with each phase. In pleadings, the opening paperwork, you track service and set up the files. In discovery, when both sides have to show their cards, you gather data and prepare the client.

And in trial prep, you line up schedules and pull the final medical records.

Now, three discovery tools. Interrogatories are written questions answered under oath. Requests for production demand documents. And requests for admission, RFAs, demand that we admit or deny a statement.

Every filing creates a docket entry, which is a line on the court's record, and its clock runs whether or not that email ever reached you.

So picture the Case Manager who shrugs and says, “I never got it.” The court's answer? “Not my problem.” Don't be that Case Manager, {name}.

Think of a docket clock like a parking meter. It runs whether you saw the ticket or not.
theory.ask: {name}, of those three tools, which one do you think is the most dangerous to ignore, and why?

frame.say:
Here's the whole lawsuit in three phases. Guess first, {name}: which phase eats most of a Case Manager's time? Hold onto that.

Phase one is pleadings. The Complaint is filed, the defendant is served, the Answer comes back, and you're tracking service and setting up the files.

Phase two is discovery: interrogatories, requests for production, and depositions, which are recorded interviews under oath. You calendar every response, gather the data and meet with the client.

Phase three is trial prep: expert reports, motions, then trial or settlement. You coordinate schedules and update the final medicals.

And the answer is discovery, almost every time. A Case Manager I trained called it “the season where every envelope has a stopwatch in it.”

Know which phase you're in, and you know what your desk should look like this week. Oh, and e-filing portals? They always seem to crash at 11:59 p.m. on the last day. Only on the last day.

Know your phase, and you know your week.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which phase is he in right now, and how can you tell from the file itself?

rules.say:
First rule, and it's a big one: litigation isn't just a longer negotiation. From the 09/24/2026 filing, the court sets the pace.

Before Atty. Thorne signs the Complaint, you check the filing date against the SOL, the deadline to sue, and you confirm the defendant's exact legal name.

Service is the proof the defendant knew he was sued, so log every attempt. Still unserved at day 14, that was 10/08/2026, and you escalate for Skip-Trace authority.

A Skip-Trace is a paid professional search for someone's current address, so Atty. Thorne approves it first. Smith was served 10/14/2026.

Now, the paper I warned you about: the RFAs. Leave one unanswered past its deadline and it may be deemed admitted, meaning the court treats it as true. That's the paper that answers itself.

When discovery lands, calendar it that day and book a Discovery Intake Meeting. You could mail John Doe all 70 requests with a note saying “fill these out.” Please don't. Sit down with him, one request at a time.

You track and draft; Atty. Thorne decides and signs. And you never tell John Doe how to answer. {name}, that one's not negotiable.

Unanswered RFAs answer themselves. Calendar them the day they land.
rules.ask: {name}, an RFA lands on your desk at 4:55 on a Friday. What do you do before you go home?

model.say:
This master timeline has a trick hidden in it, and {name}, I want you to find it.

It runs from 09/24/2026 to 01/13/2027, and each numbered badge is a trigger: the Complaint filed, Smith served on 10/14, the Answer on 11/12, discovery mailed 12/01, the Scheduling Order on 12/10, and our own set e-served 12/14.

From every trigger, a line drops to its due date. Okay, here's the trick. The 12/01 line is drawn in three steps.

Plus 30 days, plus 3 days because it came by mail, and then Sunday rolls to Monday, landing on 01/04/2027. Skip any one of those steps and you're a day early or, worse, a day late.

Over on the right is the warning I want burned into your brain: 15 RFAs, and unanswered means deemed admitted. Along the bottom sit the five numbered litigation sub-folders.

Every date on our calendar is a calculation anyone can re-check. Honestly, that's what makes the defense take us seriously.

A date without its math is just a guess with a calendar icon.
model.ask: {name}, pick the 12/01 trigger and rebuild its due date out loud, step by step. What's each step for?

job.say:
So here's how it plays out on the job. Atty. Thorne authorizes suit.

Before he signs, you confirm Robert Smith's exact legal name from an independent record, like the Declaration Page or DMV records, not the Police Report alone.

I once saw a complaint use the defendant's middle name as his last name, because somebody copied it off a crash report in a hurry. It took weeks to fix. Weeks.

Ours is filed 09/24/2026, well inside our 02/04/2028 internal hard date. It's logged in the Pleadings Log, with the stamped complaint in 01_PLEADINGS the same day.

A service attempt fails? Log it. At day 14, 10/08/2026, you escalate to Atty. Thorne with the attempt log, and run the Skip-Trace once he approves.

When the RFAs land, you calendar each response with the math written in, and alert him within the hour, time-stamped.

Why so strict, {name}? Because one deemed admission can hand the defense the very fact our whole case depends on.

Get the name right, log every attempt, and calendar every RFA within the hour.
job.ask: {name}, why doesn't the Police Report alone count as proof of Robert Smith's legal name?

dodont.say:
Okay, the litigation calendar in two lists.

Do write the trigger, the service method and the arithmetic into every entry. Defendant's discovery hit John Doe by U.S. mail on 12/01/2026, so it's thirty days plus three for mail, which lands on Sunday 01/03/2027 and rolls to Monday 01/04.

Do ask the three baseline questions in every interrogatory set. And record John Doe's answers in his own words, not a tidier version of them.

The Don'ts. A perfect Complaint filed one day after the SOL. Letting a court deadline slide the way an adjuster's might. And counting the trigger day as day one.

Anybody can put a date on the calendar. The Case Manager I want puts the date and the math, so anyone can check it at midnight. Adjusters forgive. Courts mostly don't.

{name}, which of these Don'ts have you seen happen? {name}, how was it caught, and {name}, would you have caught it?

Your mystery: on this timeline, one response is due on a date that looks wrong but is actually right. Find it and prove it before the next lesson.

Date plus math, every time.
dodont.ask: {name}, which rule on this slide is most likely to get broken on a litigation calendar, and why?

why.say:
Would you rather: an adjuster's letter with ten deadlines, or one page from a judge with six? {name}, pick one and tell me why.

My answer? I'll take the adjuster every time, because the judge's page is the one nobody gets to argue with.

This is the Scheduling Order, entered 12/10/2026, and it now runs John Doe's case to a 09/13/2027 trial calendar. Think of it as the judge's calendar for the case: every big deadline, from experts to trial, in one order nobody can ignore.

Every date in it is absolute. So how do we keep any of them from sneaking up on us? Two tools.

A trial-prep checklist turns each date into a task somebody owns. And KPIs, which are just measurable scores, prove week by week that each task is ahead of its deadline.

The order sets the dates, the checklist assigns them, and the numbers show we're winning the race. Oh, and one KPI on this list is something most firms never track. It's the one that saves trials. Stick with me.

Remember it this way: the order sets it, the checklist owns it, the KPI proves it.
why.ask: {name}, why does one page signed by a judge outrank every adjuster letter in this file?

theory.say:
Four ideas, nice and simple. Trial preparation is gathering the final pieces so Atty. Thorne walks into court fully armed.

Discovery is the heavy lifting, both sides showing their cards, and it's where most of your time goes.

A deposition is an interview under oath, recorded by a court reporter. You own the logistics, never the testimony.

And because a lawsuit can take one to three years, we rerun the records and bills, so the jury sees the total cost of the injury, not a snapshot from before suit.

To keep all of it honest, we run a weekly KPI audit, like a process server assigned within 48 hours.

Speaking of records: send a subpoena and some custodian will call you back to say they've “never heard of” a patient who was there for three months. That's why we track everything with a date, {name}. Proof beats memory.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four have you already seen show up on John Doe's file, and where?

frame.say:
Phase three really comes down to three jobs. Guess first, {name}: which one do attorneys complain about most when it's done badly?

Job one is the final run. You rerun records from every provider, and you never just reuse the package from before suit, because a year-old record tells a year-old story.

Job two is subpoena management. A subpoena is the court's order that makes someone produce records or show up. You draft trial subpoenas for the witnesses Atty. Thorne names. He picks the witnesses, not you.

Job three is the trial binder. You index and tab every exhibit so, at the counsel table, he can put his hand on any document in seconds.

And the answer? The binder. I once watched an attorney flip through an untabbed binder in front of a jury for almost a full minute. The jury noticed. Juries always notice.

A binder that's just a stack helps nobody. A binder that works like a map wins arguments.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file today, which of these three jobs is already in motion?

rules.say:
The Scheduling Order controls, full stop. Pin it to the front of the file with 30-, 14- and 7-day alerts on every date.

That's our experts 03/15/2027, theirs 04/15/2027, mediation by 03/31/2027, discovery closing 05/28/2027, pretrial 08/12/2027 and trial calendar 09/13/2027.

Every extension goes in writing. Once Atty. Thorne agrees, you draft the same-day confirmation for his signature, in his name.

Two traps to dodge. One is treating court deadlines like adjuster deadlines. The other is letting the client talk to the other side. If Keystone or a defense investigator reaches John Doe, step in and tell Atty. Thorne that day.

For the 02/18/2027 deposition, you handle the reporter, the link, the tech check and the packet by 02/11/2027. Prepare the process, never the testimony.

And here's that KPI I promised. Every KPI gets a formula and a target, because “stay on top of it” isn't a measure. {name}, that's the one most firms skip.

A KPI needs a number and a deadline, or it's just a hope.
rules.ask: {name}, defense counsel will spend John Doe's deposition on the 14-Day Gap. What's your job before 02/18/2027, and where does it stop?

model.say:
This is what being ahead actually looks like. {name}, count the milestones with me.

Across the top is the runway, from 01/20/2027 to 09/13/2027, with seven of them: the deposition on 02/18, our experts 03/15, mediation by 03/31, defense experts 04/15, discovery closing 05/28, pretrial 08/12 and the trial calendar 09/13.

Before each one, three little ticks for the 30, 14 and 7-day alerts. See the red band dropping from 05/28? Nothing that needs an answer gets scheduled past it.

Underneath are nine KPIs in three families, and every one has a target you can measure, like 48 hours, 1 hour, 7 days or 10 days.

Here's the thing: a KPI without a target is a wish. “Stay on top of RFAs” is a wish. “Every RFA calendared within one hour of receipt” is a KPI.

And a file that hits its targets is a file the defense can't catch napping, which is exactly what brings a better number at mediation.

No target, no KPI. That's the line to remember.
model.ask: {name}, how would you rewrite “stay on top of RFAs” so it actually becomes a KPI?

job.say:
Let's do a week in the life. The Scheduling Order is entered 12/10/2026. You pin it to the file, calendar all six dates with three alerts each, that's 18 alerts, and file the order in 01_PLEADINGS.

Then Atty. Mercer's office calls, and an extension gets agreed by phone. It's tempting to hang up, say “great, we're good,” and move on.

Instead, you confirm Atty. Thorne actually approved it, draft the written confirmation for his signature, send it that same day in his name, and recalendar. No Scheduling Order date moves without a court order.

A Case Manager I knew once trusted a handshake extension. Three weeks later, opposing counsel “didn't recall” it. Funny how that works.

Then the deposition is noticed. You book the reporter, the link and the tech check, and send the attorney-approved packet by 02/11/2027, confirming John Doe got it.

And every week you run the docket audit, every KPI with its formula, target and dated reading, and every miss gets routed. {name}, that weekly habit is the whole game.

If it isn't in writing, it didn't get agreed.
job.ask: {name}, opposing counsel says “we'll paper the extension later.” What do you send, and when?

dodont.say:
Trial prep, in two lists.

Do call every litigation client at least every 30 days, even when nothing's happening. John Doe went quiet once already; we don't give him a reason to again. Do subpoena only the witnesses Atty. Thorne names. And do put the subpoena audit on a recurring 10-day reminder.

The Don'ts. A phone-only extension, which is just a memory nobody shares. Trial binders built from the pre-lit records, before the litigation updates came in. And sending John's prep packet the day before, when he has no time to read it.

A so-so file has the dates. A great file has the dates, the owners, the alerts and the proof that each one was met.

{name}, which of these Don'ts have you seen happen? {name}, who got blamed for it, and {name}, who should have?

Your mystery: on the trial-prep checklist you'll audit later today, at least one date was copied from the calendar before it was corrected. Spot it faster than anyone in the room.

Dates, owners, alerts, proof. Four things, every line.
dodont.ask: {name}, in your own words, what turns a date on a calendar into a date someone actually owns?

case.say:
It's 01/05/2027, Track B, the road where the case went to suit. Quick bet before I show you anything.

{name}, how many mistakes can a three-month-old Pleadings Log collect if nobody checks it? Throw out a number.

Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417 is three months old. The docket calendar was audited and corrected on 12/10/2026, but nobody reconciled the CMS Pleadings Log to it, and now the check shows five mismatches.

The executed Affidavit of Service, filed 10/16/2026, is still sitting in an Allied Process Services email with no row. That's the process server's sworn statement that Smith was handed the lawsuit, our only proof he was served.

The Interrogatories and RFPs mailed 12/01/2026 share one row that still says due 12/31/2026, while the calendar shows 01/04/2027. And there's no row at all for the 15 RFAs.

The Scheduling Order is saved as scan_1210.pdf. And a Certificate of Service dated 01/04/2027 sits in Documents, unlogged. That's our signed line saying when and how we sent papers to the other side.

Here's the lesson hiding in this mess: a log nobody reconciles slowly turns into fiction.

If you've ever named a file scan_1210, don't worry, we've all got one. Okay, ninety seconds. Find what's wrong.
case.ask: {name}, in ninety seconds, how many problems can you find in this log as it stands?

task.say:
Here's your job. Repair the Pleadings Log and Discovery Calendar for 26-CV-04417, working in CMS under Litigation, Calendar and Documents.

Add every missing row, recompute each response date from its trigger and its method of service, and write the math right into the row.

File each document in its numbered sub-folder with a proper name, and calendar the Scheduling Order's six dates.

Then the graded call. The RFA deadline never had its own row, and it's passed. Prove compliance from that Certificate of Service, record the misses honestly, and report to Atty. Thorne today.

Partway through, Jenna Price, Atty. Mercer's paralegal, will call. Log her words exactly, with the time, take no position, tell her only that Atty. Thorne will respond, and route it to him.

{name}, you're on the Certificate. {name}, you're on the RFA row. And remember, quietly hiding the miss is the easy fix. Showing it, with the proof, is the one that protects us.

Fix the date, write the math, and never hide a miss.
task.ask: {name}, the log said 12/31/2026, which was too early. Why fix a date that could only have made us early?

check.say:
Before you log this, let's go row by row, and yes, I'm calling on people.

{name}, is there an affidavit row, personal service 10/14/2026 by Allied Process Services, filed 10/16/2026, saved in 02_SERVICE_DOCS?

Did you correct the Interrogatories and RFPs to 01/04/2027 with the count written out: 12/01 plus 30, plus 3 for mail, Sunday rolled to Monday? The 15 RFAs need their own row with a red deemed-admission flag.

Is the Certificate of Service logged and checked, signed verification attached? Smith's responses go on 01/13/2027, with no extra 3 days for e-service on this file.

E-service just means papers sent electronically, and whether it adds days depends on the court's rules, which Atty. Thorne confirms.

The Scheduling Order renamed, filed in 01_PLEADINGS, all six dates in. And the late rows recorded as misses, not back-dated. Back-dating is the one thing that turns a mistake into a problem nobody can fix.

A miss you record is a mistake. A miss you back-date is a cover-up.

Your mystery for the next activity: one date on the trial-prep checklist is still from the old calendar. {name}, hunt it down.
check.ask: {name}, explain why the e-served set doesn't get three extra mail days, and who confirms that rule?

case.say:
It's 01/20/2027, and a notice just landed. {name}, before I read it, guess what's being scheduled.

Here it is: John Doe's deposition, 02/18/2027, 10:00 a.m., by videoconference, with Riverton Court Reporting. The link comes from the reporter, and they want us to confirm attendance.

Now the problem. Our trial-prep checklist was drafted from the calendar as first keyed, before the 12/10/2026 audit, and nobody ever reconciled it.

It shows our expert disclosure on 04/15/2027, lists mediation 03/31/2027 as if that's the session date, plans records subpoenas for June 2027, and sources the final records run from the old Demand Package.

There are no alerts and no deposition tasks. Smith's responses came in 01/13/2027 and were never docketed, and there's no KPI tracker at all.

Honestly, a wrong checklist is worse than no checklist, because people trust it. So put it beside the Scheduling Order and find the first wrong date.
case.ask: {name}, which date on the checklist is wrong first, what should it read, and what does the error risk?

task.say:
Here's what you'll do. In the CMS, audit the checklist line by line against the 12/10/2026 Scheduling Order. Every date right, every task with an owner, each with 30-, 14- and 7-day alerts.

Add the 02/18/2027 deposition logistics and the prep document set.

Then build the KPI tracker in CMS under Litigation: all nine KPIs, each with its formula and target, this file's reading with its source, and met, missed or open.

Close with one task each for the three review lenses: coverage, treatment and liability. Think of them as three pairs of glasses. Is there money to pay, is the care documented and on track, and can we prove who caused the crash?

{name}, you're on the dates. {name}, you're on the KPIs. The graded call is choosing which two items go to Atty. Thorne first.

And fair warning, e-filing portals have a sixth sense for the moment you're in a hurry. Build your alerts so you're never filing at 11:59 p.m. A checklist with tasks is fine. One with owners, alerts and proof is what we want.

Every date gets an owner, three alerts and a source.
task.ask: {name}, which two items go to Atty. Thorne first, and why those two?

model.say:
Here's the reference model, and {name}, count the corrections with me as we go.

On the left is the checklist with its faulty lines numbered. Our experts on 04/15/2027 get struck through and corrected to 03/15/2027. Mediation 03/31 becomes completed by 03/31.

The records subpoenas get dragged back from June across the red 05/28/2027 cutoff, the final records run is re-sourced from the providers, and the blank deposition block fills in.

On the right is the KPI tracker, five columns: KPI, formula, target, reading and status, with green, red and amber chips. Each corrected checklist line connects to the KPI it moves.

And in the corner, the line I want you to remember: no record means not done.

So why does this matter so much? A subpoena served in June, after discovery closes, brings back records the jury may never see. One wrong month can cost John Doe his best evidence.

One wrong month on a checklist can cost John his best evidence.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think each corrected checklist line is tied to a specific KPI?

check.say:
Check before you log it. {name}, our expert date should now read 03/15/2027, with 04/15/2027 kept as the defense date. Mediation says completed by 03/31/2027.

Records subpoenas return before 05/28/2027, and 04/28/2027 is flagged as the last day to e-serve a 30-day request, confirmed with Atty. Thorne. All six dates carry three alerts, 18 in all.

The deposition notice is docketed by 01/22/2027, the reporter confirmed, calendars aligned and the packet set for 02/11/2027.

Your Gap Record lists the documents: the EMS report, the Northgate attendance, the texts to Margaret, the MRI read, the Causation Letter. And nothing scripted for John Doe. Nothing.

Nine KPIs with formula, target, sourced reading and status. And Smith's 01/13/2027 responses logged as a docket miss and routed.

Facts and documents go in the Gap Record. Never a script.

Now your mystery for the Learning Check. John Doe goes quiet before his deposition. {name}, what's your first move, and who hears about it?
check.ask: {name}, in your own words, what's the difference between a Gap Record and a script for John?

questions.say:
Welcome to the Learning Check, game-show edition. Every answer comes from John Doe's file, in your own words, typed right under the question. {name}, you're our first contestant.

Question 1 is the gate, so take it slowly. Work the 12/01/2026 response date step by step.

Then explain how the count changes for a set e-served by consent, meaning both sides agreed in writing to trade papers electronically, and tell me why you'd confirm the court's rule.

If your answer is 12/31/2026 or 01/03/2027, that's the buzzer. Stop and rework the count before you go on.

After that, name Atty. Mercer's three defenses and the evidence on file you'd pull against each, and tell me where the affidavit, the RFAs and the Scheduling Order get filed and named.

No phone-a-friend, but you can phone the calendar. And no, the cousin who's “basically a paralegal” doesn't count either.

The count is three steps every time: trigger, plus days, then roll the weekend.
questions.ask: {name}, before you start, what are the three steps in counting from a mailed trigger?

summary.say:
Now the self-summary, in your own words. But first, picture this: opposing counsel wants two weeks at 4:45 p.m. and says they'll paper it later. Who can say yes?

Only Atty. Thorne, and only in writing, the same day.

A Case Manager I trained once said “sure, no problem” on a call like that, just to be friendly. Friendly cost us three weeks of arguing.

Okay, your scenario. It's 01/28/2027. John Doe has been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect Margaret's Civic.

Write your next five actions in order, and next to each one, who owns it. Be specific about what's yours and what goes to Atty. Thorne.

“Call John again” isn't an answer, it's a shrug. I want five steps, five owners, and a reason for the order. {name}, I'll read yours first.
summary.ask: {name}, opposing counsel wants two weeks at 4:45 p.m. and will paper it later. Who can say yes, and what happens if nobody writes it down?

scale.say:
Last step. Rate yourself on each competency from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review.

I'll compare your rating with your score. So if you gave yourself a 5 on deadlines but missed the count in Question 1, we'll talk about that gap. It's not a gotcha, I promise. It's how we find what to practice next.

And remember, UPL, giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer, is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach.

An honest rating today is a better coaching plan tomorrow.

Here's your mystery for the Property Damage check coming up next. The Civic's screen had a number untouched since April that was wrong in two directions at once.

{name}, can you name it, and both directions, without looking?
scale.ask: {name}, where do you expect the biggest gap between your self-rating and your score?

why.say:
Remember the question from Day 1? Does Property Damage touch our case? Well, it's back, and this time there's money on the table.

Quick true or false, hands up for true. Keystone offering Margaret $792.00 for her Civic lowers John Doe's settlement. {name}, true or false?

False. Margaret's Loss of Use and Diminished Value are her own claim, on the separate file the firm opened for her, paid from Keystone's $25,000 Property Damage limit, outside John's $40,000 stack. His numbers don't move.

But here's the catch. Three things from that file can still reach him: a release worded too widely, the photos and estimates already in his severity set, and the rental dates behind his gap.

So today's job is telling which is which, and routing.

Margaret's car money is her own claim. John's numbers don't move, but watch the release.

And the red flag on PD at settlement. Keystone's release covers "all claims arising from" the 02/06/2026 accident. That can reach John's BI suit. Nothing gets accepted, rejected or countered. The release goes to Atty. Thorne.
why.ask: {name}, of those three, which one could hurt John Doe the most if nobody caught it?

rules.say:
Let me paint two Case Managers. The first sees a car offer, figures it has nothing to do with John, and forwards the paperwork to whoever asked.

The second reads the release before the numbers. Keystone's 12/10/2026 release covers all claims arising from the 02/06/2026 accident and asks Mr. Doe to sign. Uh-oh.

A Property Damage release must never release the injury claim. So you check the claim number, KM-26-440871-PD for the car against KM-26-440871 for John, you hold it, and you route it to Atty. Thorne the same day.

John signs nothing. Keep the photos, the estimate and the $2,315.00 supplement identical on both files, and the rental dates too.

And never accept, reject, counter or value a car figure. {name}, be the second Case Manager.

Read the release before the numbers, every time.
rules.ask: {name}, the release says Mr. Doe. Which Mr. Doe could sign it, and why does that worry us?

job.say:
Here's how it plays out on the job. Keystone sends a release: you check its scope and claim number, hold it, and escalate it to Atty. Thorne in Tasks. Nobody gets asked to sign.

Keystone restates its figure: you log it on Margaret's Property Damage file, and John's Net Sheet doesn't change by a penny.

Defense counsel asks for the car documents in discovery: you confirm the severity set and the rental dates match the Property Damage file, page by page.

I once saw a release signed in a parking lot because the client wanted lunch. Nobody wants that story, {name}.

A small thing today, a release held for one afternoon, protects the whole injury case.
job.ask: {name}, Keystone moves its offer up. Explain what changes on John Doe's Net Sheet, and why?

task.say:
Your task has five moves. First, read the release, its scope and its claim number, before you look at a single dollar figure.

Second, hold it and route it to Atty. Thorne in Tasks, escalated the same day.

Third, sort each outcome: the release, the Diminished Value figure, the Loss of Use figure, the severity set and the rental dates. For each one, does it reach John's settlement or stay on Margaret's file, and why, in one line.

Fourth, take Leah Moran's call, and accept nothing, reject nothing, counter nothing.

Fifth, write Atty. Thorne a short memo that ends in one line: does this touch John's case, and how? {name}, I'll read yours first.

Scope first, dollars second, Atty. Thorne decides.
task.ask: {name}, what will you say when Leah asks if Mr. Doe will just sign today?

case.say:
It's 12/10/2026, and an email just landed from Leah Moran at Keystone's Property Damage desk. Before I open it, {name}, guess what's attached. A check?

Nope. A release. Keystone's final position on Margaret's Civic is $792.00 for Diminished Value and $0 for Loss of Use.

And the release covers all claims arising from the 02/06/2026 accident, for Mr. Doe to sign so payment can go out. She's calling this afternoon.

Meanwhile, John's injury suit is in discovery, and Atty. Thorne wants to know what any of this changes for John.

theory.say:
The defense has a simple goal in a deposition: get the client to contradict himself, lose his temper or exaggerate, because each one chips away at his credibility. General rules protect against that. A script can't.

So let's reset some expectations. Defense counsel may ask very broad questions, and wide questions are normal, not attacks.

There's a real difference between an estimate and a guess. An estimate rests on what you saw or felt. A guess claims what you couldn't know. Only the estimate is honest testimony.

A deposition is information gathering, not a battle. Nothing gets won there, so the smallest target protects the case. And when Atty. Thorne objects, that's a formal flag on the record protecting the witness, not a sign of trouble.

Now, the over-sharer problem, in one story. A client of ours was asked, “What time did you leave the house?”

He answered with the time, his breakfast, his feud with the neighbor's dog, and the fact that he'd had “maybe one beer the night before.” Nobody asked about the beer. {name}, which rule would have saved him?

frame.say:
These are the seven Golden Rules for testifying. Before I reveal them, {name}, guess which one clients break most often. Hold it.

Rule one, always tell the absolute truth, because a damaged case can be saved and a lied-about one can't.

Rules two and three: pause two full seconds, then answer in words. That buys time to think, gives a clean transcript, and opens a window for Atty. Thorne to object.

Rules four and five: never guess, and answer only what was asked, then stop. “I don't know” is a complete answer, and it keeps the target small.

Rules six and seven: hold the silence after you've answered, and don't try to win.

The answer to my guess is rule five. Every lawyer in America has said “just answer the question” so often it should be printed on their business cards.

These are general rules. We teach every client the same seven, and none of them tells John what to say.

Truth, pause, words, no guessing, short, silence, don't argue. Seven rules, zero scripts.

Rule one is the truth, and the prior-injury question is the Liar's Trap; counsel usually has the records already. Pause two seconds and answer in words, since the court reporter can't type a nod.

Never guess, answer only what's asked, then hold the silence and don't argue.

The “Is that all” trap can fence off the hand numbness, and the complete record, not memory, is the full list. Compound questions fold two facts into one yes, and John can say a question's unclear.

On an objection, John stops, then answers unless he's told not to. The EMS report, MRI and EDR are Atty. Thorne's to use.

After suit, the defense went after fault and mitigation. The seatbelt is comparative fault, which means blaming John for part of his own injuries. The missed visits are failure to mitigate, which means saying he didn't do enough to get better.

And here's the difference that matters. Fault can reduce or even wipe out recovery. Mitigation only cuts the damages the missed care actually caused.

Funny thing about crashes: I've never once met a driver who thought it was their fault. Ten cars, ten witnesses, ten people sure it was the other guy.

That's why we answer every allegation with a document, not an opinion.
why.ask: {name}, which of Smith's three allegations isn't about John's own conduct at all?

theory.say:
Before I give you the ideas, {name}, guess: if a jury says John is 20% at fault, does he always get 80% of his damages? Hold that.

Comparative negligence splits fault between the people involved, and the share charged to the injured person can reduce, or even bar, what they recover.

There are three systems, pure, modified and contributory, and they treat the very same finding differently. So it's the state's rule, not the percentage alone, that decides the money. The answer to my guess: not always.

Next, liability status: accepted, partial or denied, recorded with its source, so Atty. Thorne sees what's still being fought over.

And keep fault and mitigation in separate boxes. Comparative fault is about the crash. Failure to mitigate is about later care, and it only trims damages that could have been avoided.

All of this feeds the counter-package, which is just an index that answers each defense claim with evidence that can actually be used in court.

Fault is about the crash, mitigation is about the care, and the state's rule sets the money.
theory.ask: {name}, why doesn't the percentage of fault, on its own, tell us what John recovers?

frame.say:
Here's the counter-package laid out, one allegation per row. {name}, follow along.

Unbelted passenger: that's about John's seatbelt, and the EDR shows the belt buckled while the EMS report reads restrained front-seat passenger.

Failure to mitigate: the 19 days without visits, 04/02 to 04/21/2026. That's answered by the A-C-T record and its documented cause, the anxiety after the crash, in Dr. Reyes's 04/20 note and the counselor's 06/10 summary.

And causation, the 14-Day Gap and the degenerative MRI, answered by the Gap Record: four reasons, the EMS neck complaint and the Causation Letter.

Every allegation, a document. That's the whole idea.
frame.ask: {name}, which row do you predict the defense will lean on hardest, and which document answers it?

rules.say:
Now the rules. Comparative negligence splits fault. Under pure, damages fall by John's share, however large.

Under modified, they fall, but recovery is barred at 50% in some states or 51% in others. Under contributory, any fault at all bars recovery. Confirm the governing rule with Atty. Thorne.

The out-of-turn allegation targets Kevin Alvarez, and whatever the defense says about him, the stack stays $40,000. Unbelted is answered by the EDR and the EMS report. Failure to mitigate trims only avoidable damages, and the A-C-T record answers it.

Evidence counts only if it can come in, meaning it's allowed in court. So record source, witness and custody, meaning who held it and when. Don't rest on the citation alone.

You gather and index; Atty. Thorne decides fault, admissibility and coverage. {name}, here's the bottom line: every point of fault we can't answer comes straight out of John's check.

Evidence without a witness is just a piece of paper.
rules.ask: {name}, if a jury finds John 20% at fault, what does he recover under each of the three systems?

Under contributory, he's barred either way. Under a modified 50% rule, he's barred at 50%. That's the cliff. One percentage point, and a whole recovery falls off it.

On the right are the three allegations, each pointing to its answer already in the file. Out of turn: RPD-26-018842, Calloway and the video. Unbelted: EDR buckled and EMS restrained. Failed to mitigate: the A-C-T record from 04/08 to 04/23.

Along the bottom, a reminder: the stack stays $40,000.

Source, witness, custody. Three answers for every exhibit.

dodont.say:
The liability counter-package, in two lists.

Do answer each allegation with a document, not an argument. The defense says the Escape entered the stop out of turn; we answer with the doorbell-camera video and the Police Report, not a strongly worded paragraph. And do read the damage pattern together with the video and the witness.

The Don'ts. Telling John he “can't be blamed” because he was a passenger. That's an opinion on liability, and it's Atty. Thorne's, not ours. And adding Kevin Alvarez's policy to the stack just because the defense blames him. Pointing a finger at Kevin doesn't open a new layer.

The lazy reply is “we disagree.” The reply I want is one allegation, one document, one page cite, all the way down.

{name}, which of these Don'ts have you seen happen? {name}, who said it to the client?

Your mystery for the next lesson: two people disappear on this file, months apart. One of them is on our side. Same problem, completely different rules. Come ready to tell me why.

Document beats argument, every single time.

why.say:
Here's the mystery I left you with: two people went missing on this file. Quick game first. I'll describe one of them, you shout “Smith” or “John.”

What do they share? Neither one has a working contact point. What's different? One's the opponent and one's our client, and who's allowed to do what follows from that.

The tools overlap: Skip-Trace, the process server, certified proof of notice. A Skip-Trace is a search of records to find someone's current address. A process server is the person who hands over the court papers.

Now, if you've watched TV, you think a skip-trace means a dark room, six monitors and someone yelling “enhance.” In real life it's a database search, a permission form and a lot of waiting.

Either way, the record we keep is what proves we did our job.

And the red flag on service. Robert Smith still unserved fourteen days after filing, 10/08/2026. A fourth knock just burns time toward the 01/22/2027 deadline. You escalate to Atty. Thorne for skip-trace authority.
why.ask: {name}, Smith and John both went missing. What do they share, and what's different about them?

theory.say:
Filing a lawsuit means nothing until service, which is the defendant being formally handed the papers. No service, and the case stalls and can be dismissed.

Defendants who know a suit is coming may hide, ignore the door or move. That's why diligent, logged attempts matter: they prove the effort.

{name}, guess what a logged failed attempt is worth compared to a successful one. Hold it.

When an address goes stale, there's the Skip-Trace, a background search of utility, employment and address records, run only for a permissible purpose, meaning a legal reason the law allows.

If someone's still dodging, there's alternative service, a court-approved substitute like mail or posting on the door, and only the attorney can ask for it.

On the client side, certified notice gives us proof of mailing, and paired with email, it shows John was told how to respond.

And the answer to my guess: almost as much. A failed attempt, logged with date, time and address, is the evidence a judge needs to approve the next step.

Log every attempt. A failed knock on paper still moves the case.
theory.ask: {name}, why is a logged failed attempt worth almost as much as a successful one?

frame.say:
Here's the evading defendant protocol, step by step. When attempts fail, you log each one's date, time and address and follow up with the server every five days.

If the address looks stale, then on Atty. Thorne's authority, a Skip-Trace runs through licensed databases checking utility, employment and active-address records.

With the right address and the person still dodging, the server varies the windows, early mornings, evenings and weekends, where the court's rules allow. If that still fails, Atty. Thorne may ask the court to permit alternative service by mail or posting.

And when service finally happens, the signed affidavit of service, the server's sworn statement that the papers were delivered, gets filed with the court. Never leave it sitting in an email.

“The server's handling it” isn't tracking. Tracking is knowing every attempt by date and calling the server on day five, not day thirty.

{name}, I once had a defendant who answered the door, took the papers, and said “I'm his twin brother.” He wasn't. The server's notes described his tattoo. Details win.
frame.ask: {name}, on Smith's service, which of these five steps did we actually need?

rules.say:
Now the rules, with the real dates. The clerk issues the Summons, the process server gets the papers, you follow up every five days, and the affidavit is filed: here 09/24 filed, 10/14 served, 10/16/2026 affidavit.

The Summons, by the way, is the court's official notice telling the defendant he's been sued and how long he has to answer.

Three failed attempts at 118 Larkspur Ln and a neighbor saying Smith moved means a stale address. So Skip-Trace first, permissible purpose only. On 10/09 it found 4410 Quarry Ridge Ct, Millbrook.

For John, silent since 01/22/2027, run Day 2's No Contact Protocol, our step-by-step plan for a client who goes quiet, every attempt logged. The Step 4 letter goes certified mail and email over Atty. Thorne's signature, by 01/27/2027.

Withdrawal goes in only if he directs it. And Margaret hears only that the firm needs John to call.

rules.ask: {name}, three attempts failed at 118 Larkspur Ln. Why is a fourth at 6:00 a.m. the wrong move?

why.say:
Would you rather, quick round. Would you rather tell a client their case is being dropped in a letter, or in a phone call? Letter hands up. Phone hands up.

{name}, you picked the letter. Defend it.

Okay, confession: trick question. Neither of those is your first move. Atty. Thorne talks to the client first, and the letter is never the client's first news.

A Dropped Case is a claim the firm stops pursuing before it resolves. John Doe's file never gets here, because earlier today the Skip-Trace found the people his file needed. But some cases do.

And a Withdrawal Letter is basically the politest breakup letter ever written: it's not you, it's the case.

Done carelessly, a drop leaves a client confused and the firm exposed. Done right, the file proves everyone was told.

The client hears it from the attorney first. The letter only confirms it.

There's one sentence in the client's letter that must never appear in the carrier's. I'll tell you which one shortly.

Here's the red flag on disengagement. A carrier letter that says Denise stopped treating. Only the client's letter carries the reason, in Atty. Thorne's words. Anywhere else, it's a defect.
why.ask: {name}, if a Dropped Case just went quiet in the CMS with no letters, who could get hurt by that?

theory.say:
Some vocabulary, nice and simple. A Dropped Case is a claim we stop before it's resolved, and it has to be written up, closed out and proved.

Cases get dropped for a handful of reasons. The client stops answering or pulls out. We can't show the other driver was at fault. There's no insurance money, or not enough of it.

Or the client can't finish treatment, or new facts don't match the old ones. Add one you'll see a lot: a client with no Health Plan who simply can't pay for care.

The Withdrawal Letter is the formal notice that the lawyer and client relationship is over. Pending Drop is the status that says the decision's made but the letters haven't gone out yet.

And the proof, meaning the receipts, the logs and the saved letters, is what protects the firm later.

{name}, think of a file you've seen, at work or even on TV. Which of these reasons fits it?

A drop isn't silence. It's a decision, a letter and a receipt.
theory.ask: {name}, which of those reasons do you think is the hardest one to explain to a client?

frame.say:
Three kinds of recipient, three kinds of letter, and here's the reveal I promised.

The client's letter carries the date, the date of loss, the reason in Atty. Thorne's words, and the next step he approves, which is to speak to another attorney promptly.

It goes by the client's preferred method, email, text or both, plus Certified Mail, which is mail where the post office gives us proof it was delivered.

The carrier's letter carries the date, the client's name, the date of loss and the claim number, and says only that we no longer represent the client. The medical provider's letter says the same and asks them to update their records.

Those two go by email or fax, whichever the CRM notes say that party prefers. The CRM is our contact file: who each person is and how they like to be reached.

Now look at what's missing from those two letters. The reason. That's the sentence that never travels. {name}, why not?

The reason goes to the client and nobody else.
frame.ask: {name}, what could go wrong if the carrier learned exactly why the firm withdrew?

rules.say:
Six steps, always in this order. First, the gate: the status reads Pending Drop, and there's a note from Atty. Thorne or the Case Manager that the client was told. If either is missing, nothing goes out.

Second, prepare a Withdrawal Letter for every party on the file, over Atty. Thorne's signature, saved in Word and PDF. Third, send each one by its method.

Fourth, annotate each send with party, method and date, and save the sent letter. Fifth, follow up on receipt. Sixth, switch the status to Dropped and keep the proof.

It's so tempting to just flip the status to Dropped and move on. Don't. The file has to prove every step.

War story. A Case Manager I trained got a call two years after a drop from a client swearing nobody ever told him. She pulled up the note, the logged text, and the signed green Certified Mail card. The call ended in about ninety seconds.

An unresponsive client only gets here through the No Contact Protocol, our step-by-step plan for a silent client, and this is where it ends. {name}, got it?

Gate, letters, send, log, follow up, then Dropped. Never skip ahead.
rules.ask: {name}, the status says Pending Drop but there's no note. What do you do, and who do you tell?

model.say:
Here's the whole close-out on one rail. Before I walk it, {name}, guess which step gets skipped most in a busy week. Hold that thought.

Step one, the gate, with its two ticks: Pending Drop, and the client told. Step two, the three letters, client, carrier and provider, each saved in Word and PDF.

Step three, the send: the client by her preferred method plus Certified Mail, carriers and providers by email or fax as the CRM says. Step four, annotate and save.

Step five, follow up on the return receipt, the acknowledgement and the fax confirmation. Step six, the status flips from Pending Drop to Dropped, proof kept.

Closing a file is a lot like spring cleaning. You can shove everything in the closet and shut the door. Or you label every box, so when someone opens that closet in two years, it all makes sense.

And the step that gets skipped most? Step five, the follow-up.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the follow-up on receipt is the step people skip?

job.say:
Here's how it runs on the job. The trigger is the status Pending Drop, with Atty. Thorne's note that the client was told.

You open the CMS, under Documents, where the firm's letter templates live, and prepare each party's Withdrawal Letter from the template, for his signature. Save each one in Word and PDF.

Once the letters are signed, you send each by its method, email, text, fax or Certified Mail, and you log the party, the method and the date in the Communications Log.

When the receipts are followed up, you switch the status to Dropped and file the proof in Documents: the receipts, the logs and the attorney's note.

Why all the fuss? Because a dropped file can still come back years later as a complaint, and the only thing standing between the firm and trouble is that proof.

Every file ends up as the last box in storage someday. Make sure yours is the box nobody has to worry about. {name}, you're up.
job.ask: {name}, where in the CMS would you look first to prove a client was told about the drop?

dodont.say:
The Dropped Case, in two lists.

Do check the gate before you open the template. That means Atty. Thorne has decided, in writing, before a single letter gets drafted. And do send the client's letter two ways, with one of them giving us proof it arrived.

The Don'ts. Putting the reason in a carrier's letter. They get notice that we're out, not why. Switching the status to Dropped before every letter is out and logged. And telling the client the case is worthless.

That last one isn't a style point. Whether a claim had value is Atty. Thorne's conversation, never ours.

The careless close is one email and a status change. The careful close is the gate checked, every letter sent and logged with proof, and only then the status.

{name}, which of these Don'ts have you seen happen? {name}, how did the client find out?

Your mystery for the activity: you're about to meet Denise Harlow. Her file has one detail that decides how her letter goes out, and another that explains why she's being dropped. Find both before you write a word.

Value is Atty. Thorne's conversation, never ours.
dodont.ask: {name}, if the client asks what her claim was worth, whose conversation is that, and what do you say?

case.say:
This one's a practice matter, not John Doe's file, so don't open it or create it in the CMS. It's 12/09/2026. Meet Denise Harlow.

She was rear-ended at a red light on 09/19/2026. Granite Shield Insurance has the BI claim, GS-26-48213, and the CRM, our contact records, says its adjuster, Paul Ostrander, takes email only.

She treated at Brookside Physical Therapy from 09/24 to 10/29/2026, then stopped. {name}, before I tell you why, predict it: why is Atty. Thorne dropping this case?

Here's the reveal. She has no Health Plan to pay for care, and Brookside declined a Letter of Protection, the firm's written promise to pay the provider out of any settlement. Think of it as an IOU the provider wouldn't take.

why.say:
Let's play Guess the Net. Same $40,000.00 gross on both tracks. On Track A, where Keystone settled, John Doe netted $20,359.92.

On Track B, Keystone stonewalled, so we sued, mediated and arbitrated, and Laura Whitcomb's award came in on 07/06/2027. Thumbs up if you think John nets more on Track B, thumbs down if less.

{name}, you're thumbs down? Give me a number, and tell me why you picked it.

Here's the reveal: $14,713.75. Same gross, almost six thousand dollars less in his pocket. Three things moved that number, and I'll reveal them one at a time.

And yes, when that award check lands, someone in this office will want a photo holding it like a lottery winner. Take the photo. Then it goes straight into trust.

John is going to notice the difference, and he deserves to understand every dollar before he signs anything. That's what the Net Sheet is for.
why.ask: {name}, same $40,000.00 gross on both tracks. Predict the three things that pulled John's net down, and why each one moved?

theory.say:
The Net Sheet is the page that shows the client where every dollar came from and where every dollar goes. Think of it as the receipt for the whole case. Four ideas sit under it.

One, the common fund doctrine. Everyone who gets paid out of the pot helps pay for the work that filled the pot. So a lienholder, the company that paid a Medical Bill and wants paying back, shares in our fees and costs. That's how we get reductions.

Two, the double-dipping trap: counting the same dollar twice, or paying the same bill twice. Carriers audit, so every dollar traces back to its source.

Three, fee transparency. Each stream of money carries its own fee, tracked separately.

Four, the Final Payoff Letter, a signed letter that says this amount settles the bill in full. No letter, no check.

{name}, which of those four would you bet a brand-new Case Manager forgets first, and what would it cost John?

Every dollar has a source, and every payment has a letter.
theory.ask: {name}, in your own words, why should Peach State share in the cost of a lawsuit it never filed?

frame.say:
Here's the Master Financial Ledger, top to bottom, and there's a booby trap in it. I'll tell you where at the end.

First, the recovery summary: the gross by stream, each with its source, so Keystone's BI tendered at mediation and both UM awards from arbitration.

Next, attorney fees, the fee on each stream, confirmed from the retainer. On this file that's the 40% tier because suit was filed. The retainer says a third if the case settles before suit, 40% once suit is filed, because a lawsuit is a lot more work.

Then case expenses, every cost the firm advanced, each with its receipt: filing, service, mediation, arbitration, the court reporter, records, plus the pre-suit costs.

Then the provider ledger: charges, payments, adjustments, balance owed and reduction, listing only the liens actually owed. Last, the net to the client, line by line.

The booby trap? The provider ledger, where a zero-balance line loves to sneak onto the payables. {name}, keep your eyes on that one.

The right total isn't enough. Every line needs a source.
frame.ask: {name}, which section of this ledger would you check twice on a litigated file, and what could go wrong there?

rules.say:
The award ends the case, not the work. Laura Whitcomb's 07/06/2027 award gives Harbor Point's $20,000.00 and Cardinal State's $10,000.00, and with Keystone's $10,000.00 BI from the 03/18/2027 mediation, the gross is $40,000.00.

The fee follows the retainer: suit filed 09/24/2026, so 40%, $16,000.00, confirmed by Atty. Thorne.

The fund pays only what's owed. Peach State's reduction follows the fee charged, $744.00, accepted at $1,116.00, and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepts $4,275.00. Net: $14,713.75.

Nothing leaves trust until the checks clear, the Payoff Letters are in and John signs. Copying Track A's numbers is the shortcut that bites. {name}, you rebuild every line from this file.

You explain the arithmetic. Whether suing was worth it is Atty. Thorne's conversation.
rules.ask: {name}, Peach State's reduction was $620.00 on Track A. Explain why it's $744.00 now?

Closing out the litigated file, in two lists.

The lazy close copies last month's numbers. The close I want rebuilds every figure from this file, so John's net of $14,713.75 holds up to any question he asks.

Final round of the game show, and the jackpot question is the whole case. John Doe's file is now closed, from intake all the way to the award. Take a second to appreciate that: you carried one file through every phase.

{name}, you're my lightning-round contestant: I'll ask you one of these out loud when time's up. And {name}, you're the judge. If you hear a number without a source, you buzz.

A number without a source is just a rumor.

Now your self-summary, in your own words. Keep Question 5 in mind as you write, because it's the UPL gate, the line between explaining facts and giving legal advice.

Arithmetic, yes; opinion, no. If you write that the lawsuit was or wasn't worth it, you've crossed the line, however good the rest is.

Then your scenario: it's 01/28/2027, John's been unreachable for six days, his deposition is noticed for 02/18/2027, and defense counsel wants to inspect Margaret's Civic. Give me your next five actions, in order, and who owns each one.

Why bring back an old moment? The best Case Managers I've worked with can tell you a file's whole story from memory, like a favorite movie. The ones who struggle remember only the last scene.

{name}, which kind are you going to be?

Here's your Skill Scale for the award and the Net Sheet. Score yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, then submit it for review.

I'll sit down with your rating beside your score, and if there's a wide gap either way, we'll talk it through together. Be as honest about yourself as you've been with John's numbers.

And keep your pen out, because we've got one more file to close, and it's not a winner. Denise Harlow's case is dropped.

scale.ask: {name}, looking back across John Doe's whole file, which skill do you feel strongest in now, and what proves it?

why.say:
Quick game: Who Has to Answer? I'll name someone, you shout “has to” or “doesn't have to” answer our questions right now.

Robert Smith, the defendant. The hospital's records custodian. Ruth Calloway, the witness. {name}, you take the tiebreaker on Ruth.

Here's the reveal. Robert Smith has to, because he's a party in the lawsuit. The custodian and Ruth Calloway don't, not unless the court commands it. That command is a subpoena.

It's powerful, and it comes with rules. Serve it out of order, write it too broadly, or let the records come back after discovery closes on 05/28/2027, and Atty. Thorne could walk into trial without the evidence.

And trust me, the first time you call a records department, someone will cheerfully tell you they've “never heard of” a patient whose MRI they did. Today you learn to make that call go very differently.

Parties have to answer. Everyone else needs the court to ask.

The red flag on subpoenas is three little words: "all records of any kind." That invites a Motion to Quash. One subject, an exact date range, named record types, and Atty. Thorne signs.
why.ask: {name}, who on John Doe's file holds evidence we need but owes us nothing unless the court commands it, and why?

theory.say:
Two tools, two different jobs. A Subpoena Duces Tecum, which is Latin for “bring it with you,” orders someone outside the lawsuit to produce documents, like a hospital, a phone company or an employer.

A trial subpoena orders a witness to show up and testify: fact witnesses, treating doctors, police officers. One brings paper, the other brings a person.

Now the warning. A request for “all records of any kind” is what the other side calls a fishing expedition, and they can file a Motion to Quash, which asks the court to cancel it.

The model is narrow: emergency room records, triage notes and imaging, one client, the accident date only. Ask for the ocean and you get nothing. Ask for one fish and it arrives fast.

And the order never changes: you draft, you notice opposing counsel, you serve the custodian, and you track compliance. {name}, in your own words, why does notice come first?

Narrow, noticed, then served. Every time.
theory.ask: {name}, why would a court care whether a subpoena is narrow, even when the records are about our own client?

rules.say:
Here's how it runs on John Doe's file. The trigger is a refused request, or a record Atty. Thorne needs from its custodian. You ask him whether he wants a records subpoena, and he decides, signs and issues it.

You draft on the court-approved form with the case style, Civil Action No. 26-CV-04417, the named custodian and a narrow Exhibit A: one subject, exact dates, named record types.

A copy goes to Atty. Grant Mercer first, and only after the notice period does Allied Process Services serve the custodian.

Five days before production you make the compliance call, and you pay the copy invoice promptly, because an unpaid invoice is the most popular reason records go missing. Everything comes back before 05/28/2027.

Trial subpoenas go only to the witnesses Atty. Thorne names, tasked against 08/12/2027 and 09/13/2027. {name}, why do you think we call five days before, not the day of?

He decides, you draft, notice goes first, and the records come home before discovery closes.
rules.ask: {name}, the custodian says on the compliance call that the request is too broad. What do you do, and who decides?

job.say:
Let's run one through. Atty. Thorne needs the Riverton Fire Run Report from its custodian. You route that question to him through Tasks, and you draft nothing until he decides.

Once he approves, you build it from the template with a narrow Exhibit A: run RF-26-0206-114, Medic 7, John Doe, 02/06/2026 only.

The notice to Atty. Mercer is dated before service, every single time. I once audited a file where the notice and the service had the same date, and the defense argued for a month about which happened first. Nobody wins that argument.

Then, while it's open, you review its row in the subpoena log every ten days, call the custodian five days before production, and log each reading with its date. Any miss goes to Atty. Thorne.

Why? Because a record that arrives after discovery closes may never reach the jury.

So here's your mystery, {name}: which record on John Doe's file is most likely to need a subpoena next, and why that one?
job.ask: {name}, which two dates on a subpoena log row tell you, at a glance, whether notice came first?

case.say:
Show of hands: who's ever sent an important email and then found the reply sitting in spam three days later? Keep them up. {name}, that's a lot of hands, and that's exactly why we check.

It's the twenty-second of September twenty twenty-six, and we're on Track B, the litigation track, the road where the case goes to court.

The file went to Litigation on the tenth, on Atty. Thorne's authorization, and the filing target is the twenty-fourth. So today is our forty-eight-hour audit, our two-day check that everything's ready before we file.

This morning he approved his Complaint against Robert Smith in the State Court of Riverton County. The Complaint is the document that starts the lawsuit, the starter's pistol.

What we don't have yet is the civil cover sheet and the summons, the court's notice telling Robert Smith he's being sued.

And there's a trap in the CMS: an older draft from the fifteenth, stamped not for filing, unsigned, no case number. Once the envelope is accepted, the fee tier moves to forty percent and the court's clocks start.

Two Complaints, one court. Only one of them should ever leave this building.
case.ask: {name}, two Complaints sit in the CMS today. In your own words, how will you make sure the right one reaches the court?

task.say:
Four moves. First, tag Nadia Brooks on the Litigation Desk with a task she can act on without calling you: the cover sheet and the summons, built from the Complaint he approved this morning, due tonight, routed to Atty. Thorne for signature. He signs on the twenty-third.

Second, on the twenty-fourth, you build the envelope in Court E-Filing, the court's online filing system: the caption, the court, the three documents, the filing attorney and the two hundred eighteen dollar fee. Open every page to check his signature first.

Third, when it's accepted, you record the case number, file the stamped Complaint, the summons and the conference notice, and post the fee.

And yes, check your spam folder for the acceptance email. Court systems love sending the most important message of the month straight to junk.

Fourth, you calendar what the filing starts, and you hold what it doesn't. {name}, you're Nadia; {name}, you're writing her the task.

If Nadia has to call you, the task wasn't finished.
task.ask: {name}, which deadline can you calendar the day you file, which one has to wait, and why?

check.say:
Check your work against this, and {name}, you're grading the person next to you. Your task to Nadia names the documents, the approved Complaint, the due date and Atty. Thorne as signer.

Nothing went in unsigned, and the September fifteenth draft never left the CMS. The envelope was accepted on the twenty-fourth as twenty-six CV zero four four one seven, and that number replaced Pending in the court fields.

Three named PDFs sit in zero one pleadings, and costs read seven hundred four dollars seventy-five.

The service deadline, the last day to formally deliver the lawsuit to Robert Smith, is January twenty-second, twenty twenty-seven, a Friday, a hundred and twenty days out, with alerts. Allied Process Services has its hand-off.

The conference is December tenth at nine, with Atty. Thorne attending. And the answer date says set on service, because his clock can't start until he's actually handed the papers.

A case number is just the start. The real work is every clock that number started.

Your mystery for the next block: Allied hasn't served him yet. {name}, predict it: what happens to our calendar if they can't find Robert Smith?
check.ask: {name}, if the answer date had been calendared today, what would it have been counted from, and why is that wrong?

case.say:
It's 07/30/2027, three in the afternoon, and John Doe's case is won. The award went out today, every lien paid on its Payoff Letter.

The litigation file is in the CMS: the Complaint, the service papers, the Answer, the Scheduling Order, the mediation term sheet and both binders.
